candidates.name: Repo Atlas — Triage Console
candidates.summary: A single Node process on port 4600 serves both the API and the built Vite+React SPA. It scans ~/Projects on demand into a JSON disk cache, pre-computes every domain rule server-side (attention classification, queue order, local-timezone day buckets), and ships the SPA one pre-sorted payload. The UI is two screens — overview (attention queue on top, aggregate heatmap + timeline below) and per-repo drill-down (languages/LOC, recent commits, last-touched files, branches, repo-scoped heatmap + timeline reusing the same two SVG components) — plus a Rescan button that triggers an async rescan with n/total progress and swaps data in place. One exported hook (useAtlas) owns all data flow and has the required component-mount test; scan logic is split into a pure-function domain module so the git rules are unit-testable without fixtures.
candidates.architecture: Single repo, plain ESM JavaScript throughout. Server: node:http (no framework) serving the vite-built dist plus three JSON endpoints — GET /api/repos (in-memory cache hydrated from .atlas-cache.json at boot, so first paint is instant), POST /api/rescan (kicks off async scan, returns 202), GET /api/status ({scanning, done, total}). The scanner walks ~/Projects depth-limited, skipping node_modules, detecting .git as dir or file (worktrees), then per repo shells out to git for branch, porcelain status, ahead/behind vs @{u}, last-commit, commit history timestamps, recent commits, last-touched files, and branch list; a separate file walk (excluding node_modules/dist/.git/vendored) produces LOC-by-extension. All tricky rules live in server/domain.js as pure functions and are baked into the RepoEntry shape defined in shared/contract.js: each entry carries attention.reasons (dirty/unpushed/stale), status ('no remote' is a distinct value that can never be 'unpushed'), and a heatmap map keyed by local-timezone YYYY-MM-DD author dates; /api/repos delivers the queue already sorted (dirty > unpushed > stale, ties by most-recent activity) so no client code can reorder it wrong. Frontend: no router — App.jsx holds overview-vs-selected-repo state; useAtlas.js is the only exported hook (initial fetch, rescan POST, 500ms status polling while scanning, atomic data swap on completion); Heatmap.jsx and Timeline.jsx are hand-rolled SVG components parameterized by a commit-date series, so aggregate and per-repo views are the same components fed different slices. shared/contract.js (data shapes, status constants, API paths, day-key format, CSS class vocabulary for dynamically built regions) and src/styles.css freeze in wave 1 and are never edited after, letting all wave-2 builders merge without touching each other's files.

build_order: Wave 1 (1 agent): scaffold + frozen contracts — package.json, vite.config.js, index.html, shared/contract.js, src/styles.css. After this wave these five files are never edited again.

Wave 2 (4 agents in parallel, disjoint scopes): [server engine] server/git.js, server/domain.js, server/scan.js, server/index.js, server/domain.test.js, server/scan.test.js; [app shell + data hook] src/main.jsx, src/App.jsx, src/useAtlas.js, src/useAtlas.test.jsx, src/App.test.jsx; [overview charts] src/components/AttentionQueue.jsx, src/components/Heatmap.jsx, src/components/Timeline.jsx, src/components/charts.test.jsx; [drill-down] src/components/RepoDetail.jsx.

Wave 3 (1 agent): integration only — run npm start against the real ~/Projects, verify DoD line by line (correct branch/dirty/last-commit for every repo, heatmap+timeline from real data, drill-down, rescan without restart), fix seam bugs, npm test fully green.
risks: Git edge cases in the real ~/Projects tree are the top integration risk: worktrees (.git is a file, and this very directory tree contains them), detached HEADs, repos with zero commits, and branches with no upstream. server/git.js must return null upstream (not an error and not 0-ahead) or the 'no remote is never unpushed' rule silently breaks in wave 3.
Ahead/behind parsing: rev-list --left-right --count output order is easy to invert; an inverted parse makes behind-only repos show as unpushed. Needs an explicit fixture test in scan.test.js.

LOC walk cost: dozens of repos with large trees can blow the rescan-with-progress budget if the exclusion list (node_modules, dist, .git, vendored) is applied per-file instead of pruning directories at walk time. Prune, don't filter.

Timezone bucketing tests are flaky unless the vitest run pins TZ; author-date-to-local-day is the one rule where a passing test on the build machine can still mislabel days for the user if implemented via UTC string slicing.

The polling hook's mount test (mocked fetch + timers in jsdom) is the most fiddly test in the plan — act() warnings and unresolved-promise leaks can leave vitest hanging, which violates the non-interactive npm test requirement.
npm start couples vite build to server launch; if wave 3 skips a rebuild after a frontend fix, it validates a stale dist. The integration agent must treat build-then-serve as one atomic step.
Contract drift: if any wave-2 agent edits shared/contract.js or styles.css instead of conforming to them, the zero-conflict merge property is lost. The frozen-after-wave-1 rule is load-bearing.
delight: Open localhost:4600 and the first paint — served from the disk cache in well under 2s — is already the answer: the repos with uncommitted work sit at the top with plain reason badges, before any chart draws.
Hit Rescan and keep working: the button ticks 7/34, 8/34 across the real repo set, and the page swaps to fresh data in place — no restart, no blank state.

Click any repo and the exact same heatmap and timeline you just read in aggregate redraw scoped to that one project — a year of one repo's life in the same visual language, because they are literally the same two SVG components.
Repos without a remote say 'no remote' instead of falsely nagging 'unpushed' — the queue never cries wolf, which is what makes it trustworthy enough to act on.

candidates.name: Repo Atlas — Mission Control
candidates.summary: A local mission-control dashboard that opens in under 2 seconds from a JSON cache and immediately answers "what needs my attention": a ranked queue of dirty, unpushed, and stale repos with plain-language reason badges and inline 90-day sparklines, backed by a hand-rolled SVG 12-month heatmap and activity timeline that cross-filter each other. Rescan streams per-repo progress live over SSE so rows settle in as they're scanned, a Cmd+K palette and j/k keys make every repo two keystrokes away, and per-repo drill-down shows languages, LOC, recent commits, last-touched files, and branches — all from local git only, read-only, no database.
candidates.architecture: Two processes in one repo, joined by a frozen contract module. A small Node HTTP server (port 4600) serves the built Vite+React SPA and four endpoints: GET /api/atlas (last cached Snapshot, instant), GET /api/repo/:id (drill-down detail), POST /api/rescan (kicks an async scan job), GET /api/rescan/events (SSE stream of per-repo progress events; client falls back to polling). The scanner walks ~/Projects depth-limited (skipping node_modules/dist/.git/vendored), runs git subprocesses per repo through a concurrency pool (branch, status --porcelain for dirty, rev-list vs @{u} for ahead/behind with no-upstream mapped to "no_remote", log with author dates for history/heatmap), classifies LOC by extension, and writes an atomic JSON snapshot cache to disk — boot loads the cache so first paint never waits on git. All domain rules live server-side and are encoded into the entry data shape per the playbook: each RepoEntry ships with computed attention reasons, a rank key from the frozen comparator (dirty > unpushed > stale, ties by recency), pre-bucketed local-timezone commit-per-day counts, and status enums — the client renders, never re-derives. shared/contract.js is written in wave 0 and never edited again: typedefs, status enums, the attention comparator, the CSS render-vocabulary class names for dynamically built regions, and design tokens; shared/fixtures.js is the single canonical Snapshot used by every client test, so server and client agents build against identical shapes and merge without touching each other's files. All charts are hand-rolled SVG components that take fixture-shaped props — no chart library. Vitest (jsdom + testing-library) covers a component-mount test for every exported hook, contract-lock tests, real-tmp-git-repo scanner tests, and endpoint/SSE lifecycle tests.

build_order: Wave 0 — single agent, contract freeze: package.json, vite.config.js, shared/contract.js, shared/fixtures.js, shared/contract.test.js, client/src/styles/tokens.css. After this wave these files are never edited again.

Wave 1 — four parallel agents on disjoint scopes: (A) server data layer: discover.js, gitfacts.js, loc.js, scanner.js, cache.js, scanner.test.js; (B) server HTTP: index.js, index.test.js against an injected fixture scanner; (C) client shell + hooks: index.html, main.jsx, App.jsx, api/hooks.js, api/hooks.test.jsx, RescanButton.jsx; (D) SVG charts: Heatmap.jsx, Timeline.jsx, Sparkline.jsx, charts.test.jsx — all four code purely against the frozen contract and fixtures.

Wave 2 — three parallel agents, composing wave-1 pieces: (E) Overview.jsx, AttentionQueue.jsx, StatsRow.jsx, app.css, Overview half of views.test.jsx; (F) RepoDetail.jsx + its half of views.test.jsx; (G) CommandPalette.jsx + keyboard-nav wiring + theme polish. Delighters (day-click cross-filter, palette, sparklines-in-rows) all land here, after must-haves are safe in wave 1.

Wave 3 — single integration agent: run the real server against ~/Projects, verify cached first paint, live-streaming rescan, cross-filter, and drill-down end to end; full vitest suite green; fix seams only, no new features.
risks: Git edge cases in gitfacts.js are the hardest correctness surface: detached HEAD, empty repos with zero commits, repos with an upstream that no longer exists, and the spec's no-upstream => 'no remote' (never 'unpushed') rule. Mitigation is real-tmp-repo tests in scanner.test.js covering each case, but an unanticipated repo state under the real ~/Projects can still surface in wave 3.

Heatmap timezone bucketing is ambiguous in practice: 'author date in local timezone' requires forcing git log date formatting to the server's local tz rather than the committer's recorded offset, or day counts drift at boundaries. The bucketing must live in scanner.js (server-side, tested) so both charts consume identical pre-bucketed data — if any client code re-buckets, aggregate and per-repo views will disagree.

Scan latency across dozens of repos: LOC counting is the expensive part and can blow the sub-2s feel if done naively. The design depends on the cache-first boot (never scan on GET /api/atlas) and the concurrency-pooled async rescan; if agent A skips the pool or the atomic cache write, first load or rescan will feel broken even though data is correct.

SSE is the riskiest integration seam: EventSource doesn't exist in jsdom, so useRescan must take an injectable transport with a polling fallback, and server/index.test.js must assert event ordering. If agents B and C interpret RescanEvent differently, live progress silently degrades — the frozen RescanEvent shape in shared/contract.js is the only defense, so wave 0 must fully specify it (event types, terminal event, error event).

Wave 2 styling depends on wave-1 components emitting exactly the contract's render-vocabulary class names; any improvised class name in Heatmap/AttentionQueue leaves unstyled or mis-styled regions that only show up at integration. Contract.test.js can lock the vocabulary list but not enforce usage — wave 3 needs an explicit visual pass.

npm start couples vite build to server boot; a client type/lint failure at build time blocks the whole definition-of-done command even if the server is healthy. Wave 3 must run npm start cold, not just vitest.
delight: First paint in well under 2 seconds from the disk cache, and the very first line of the screen is a verdict, not wallpaper: '3 repos need attention' with each row saying why in words — 'dirty: 4 files', 'unpushed: 2 commits', 'stale: 127 days' — ranked so the most urgent is always row one.

Hitting Rescan doesn't freeze anything: a progress bar fills as SSE events stream in and each repo row visibly settles from pending to fresh as its scan completes — the dashboard feels alive, and you can watch a dirty flag appear the moment the scanner reaches that repo.

Clicking any day cell on the 12-month heatmap cross-filters the timeline and surfaces that day's commits — 'what was I doing on March 12th' answered in one click, with both charts drawn as crisp hand-rolled SVG in a restrained two-hue palette.
Every attention-queue row carries a 90-day inline sparkline, so active-but-dirty and abandoned-and-dirty read differently at a glance without a single extra click.
Cmd+K opens a fuzzy palette that jumps to any repo's drill-down in two keystrokes; j/k/enter walk the queue; the whole dashboard is drivable without touching the mouse.

Drill-down tells a repo's story on one calm screen: language bars, recent commits, the files you touched last, and every branch — the 'wait, what state did I leave this in?' question answered before the terminal even opens.

candidates.name: Repo Atlas — Survey Folio
candidates.summary: Repo Atlas rendered as a cartographic survey folio: the dashboard is a set of numbered engraved plates ("Fig. 1 — Notices", "Fig. 2 — Commit Soundings") on cream paper (night-chart-room dark theme), with a pre-ranked attention queue of advisories on top, hand-rolled SVG heatmap/timeline/strata charts below, and a per-repo drill-down plate. A small Node server on :4600 surveys ~/Projects with git plumbing, serves a JSON cache instantly, and streams async rescan progress as a moving sounding line. Every must-have lands: full depth-limited scan with branch/dirty/ahead-behind/history/LOC, attention-first overview, aggregate and per-repo heatmap+timeline, drill-down, and live rescan without restart — plus search/sort, themes, stats row, and j/k keyboard navigation.
candidates.architecture:
Visual identity first, and the code is organized to protect it. The identity: an early-20th-century survey atlas. One paper surface (warm cream light / indigo-black dark), near-black ink, a single vermilion accent reserved exclusively for attention states, hairline rules, small-caps serif plate captions, monospace tabular figures for all data. Every panel on screen is a Plate — a frozen component that renders the ruled frame, figure number, and caption ("Fig. 3 — Gazetteer of Repositories"). Charts are pure hand-rolled SVG using engraving idioms: ink-density cells for the heatmap, an impulse/area "sounding" line for the timeline, hatched SVG-pattern strata for the language/LOC bar so it reads even in monochrome. No chart or CSS library; the entire look lives in tokens.css + Plate.tsx.

System shape: a dependency-light Node server (node:http + child_process git plumbing) on port 4600 serves the built Vite+React SPA from /dist plus a JSON API. GET /api/atlas returns the last snapshot from a disk cache (.atlas-cache.json) so first paint is instant (<2s taste bar); POST /api/rescan kicks an async survey with a bounded concurrency pool over repos, and GET /api/scan-events (SSE) streams {phase, repo, done, total} progress that the UI renders as a sweeping sounding line — data swaps in atomically when the survey completes, no restart. GET /api/repo/:id serves drill-down detail (recent commits, last-touched files, branches, per-repo daily buckets).

Contract-freeze-first (per playbook): wave 0 lands shared/contract.ts (all data shapes, API route names, SSE event shape, a dayKey(date) local-timezone bucketing helper), tokens.css (palette, type scale, and the full render-vocabulary class list for dynamic regions: .plate, .plate-caption, .advisory, .advisory--dirty/--unpushed/--stale/--no-remote, .gazetteer-row, .sounding, etc.), and Plate.tsx — then those files are never edited again. Tricky domain rules are encoded in the data shape so downstream code cannot get them wrong: the server emits attention as a pre-ranked AttentionEntry[] (dirty > unpushed > stale, ties by recency, computed in server/attention.js) and each repo carries explicit flags {dirty, aheadBy, behindBy, upstream: 'tracked'|'none', staleDays} with 'no remote' as a distinct state that can never surface as 'unpushed'. Heatmap buckets are keyed by author-date local-timezone dayKey at the server, so charts just paint.

Frontend: React SPA with two views — Overview (Fig. 1 Notices attention queue, Fig. 2 aggregate heatmap, Fig. 3 timeline, Fig. 4 stats Legend, Fig. 5 Gazetteer table with search/sort) and RepoDetail (per-repo heatmap/timeline, language strata, commits, touched files, branches), navigated by hash route so drill-down is linkable. Three exported hooks (useAtlas, useKeyboardNav, useTheme) each ship a component-mount test; charts develop against a fixtures module so the chart agent never needs the server. Tests: vitest + Testing Library for components/hooks; server tests build real throwaway git repos in temp dirs and assert dirty/ahead/stale/no-remote classification and attention ordering.

Wave 1 — Agent D (drill-down): src/views/RepoDetail.tsx, components/CommitLog.tsx, TouchedFiles.tsx, BranchList.tsx, src/styles/detail.css

Wave 2 (single integration agent): run against the real ~/Projects tree; verify cold-scan progress UX and <2s cached load; keyboard-nav and theme audit across both views; visual pass enforcing tokens-only styling (no ad-hoc colors); README.md; full vitest sweep green
risks: Git edge cases in the real ~/Projects tree will break naive plumbing: worktrees (.git is a file, and this user demonstrably uses them), detached HEAD, empty repos with zero commits, branches with deleted upstreams. server/gitFacts.js must treat every git call as fallible per-repo and degrade to a partial RepoSummary rather than failing the whole scan; scan.test.js must include a worktree and an empty-repo fixture or this ships broken.

Cold-scan wall time: 12 months of git log plus LOC classification across dozens of repos, serially, can take minutes. The design depends on bounded-concurrency child processes and LOC file/byte caps; if Agent A skips the concurrency pool, the first-run experience misses the <2s taste bar and the async-progress story collapses into a spinner.

The SSE progress seam between server/index.js and useAtlas is the classic cross-agent integration break: both sides are built from the frozen ScanEvent shape without ever talking. If wave 0 under-specifies it (terminal event, reconnect behavior, atomic swap signal), wave 2 burns the night reconciling.

Heatmap date math: author-date local-timezone bucketing plus 53-week grid alignment and month-label placement is fiddly and produces silent off-by-one-day/column bugs. Mitigation is dayKey() living in the frozen contract and chart tests asserting exact cell counts against fixtures — but only if both agents actually use dayKey rather than reimplementing.

'Unpushed' vs 'no remote' misclassification: rev-list against a missing upstream errors in ways easy to swallow into aheadBy=0 or, worse, a false 'unpushed'. The contract makes upstream a three-state field precisely so attention.test.js can pin this; the test is load-bearing, not optional.

Aesthetic drift: four parallel builders each improvising CSS yields exactly the generic admin template the design forbids. The tokens + render-vocabulary + Plate freeze is the guardrail, but wave 2 needs an explicit tokens-only audit (grep for raw hex values outside tokens.css) or the single-screenshot identity dies by a thousand ad-hoc styles.

npm start ambiguity: 'vite build then node server' means a stale dist can mask new frontend work during the night; builders must rebuild before verifying, and the definition-of-done check must run from a clean build.
delight: Open the page and the top plate is 'Fig. 1 — Notices': a typeset column of advisories ('SWARM — uncommitted changes, touched today', 'homeforge — 3 commits unpushed') with engraved reason glyphs and the only vermilion on the page. The first second answers 'what needs my attention', not commit wallpaper.

The whole dashboard reads as a survey folio — masthead 'REPO ATLAS: A Survey of ~/Projects', ruled numbered plates, small-caps serif captions, monospace tabular figures on cream paper. One screenshot is unmistakably this product and nothing else.

Hitting 'r' starts a survey, not a spinner: a hairline sounding line sweeps under the masthead while a ticker reads 'surveying prompt-spark (12/47)…', and when it completes the plates swap to fresh data in place — server never restarted, page never reloaded.
Hovering the heatmap writes the date and commit count into the plate's margin like a chart annotation — no floating tooltip chrome anywhere in the app.
A repo's language breakdown is a geological cross-section: hatched SVG strata you could read on a photocopier, with LOC counts set as depth labels.

j/k walks the Notices and the Gazetteer like an instrument, Enter drops into the repo's own plate set (its personal heatmap, sounding line, commit ledger), Esc surfaces back — hands never leave the keyboard.
Toggle 't' and the folio becomes the night chart room: indigo-black paper, phosphor-cream ink, same plates, same vermilion — a second look, not a second design.

judge.rationale: C wins on must-have completeness plus depth without sacrificing buildability. Must-haves: C is the only candidate that visibly satisfies the DoD line "every git repo under ~/Projects is listed" — its Fig. 5 Gazetteer table lists all repos with branch/state/last-commit, alongside the ranked Notices queue, aggregate + per-repo heatmap/timeline, full drill-down (CommitLog, TouchedFiles, BranchList, Strata LOC), and SSE-driven rescan; it also lands all four nice-to-haves (search/sort, themes, stats row, keyboard nav). B misses that DoD line: its overview shows only attention repos ("ranked queue of dirty, unpushed, and stale repos") and there is no repo table anywhere in the file_plan — clean/fresh repos are reachable only through a hidden Cmd+K palette, which is a listing miss (must_haves 7). A covers the must-haves (its contract's 'ok' status implies the queue carries all repos) but ships zero nice-to-haves — no search, no keyboard nav, no theme — which for an audience of "dozens of repos" hurts value and caps depth: two spartan screens whose every use is the same skeleton (depth 4). Buildability: A is cleanest (9) — smallest surface, frozen contract, one hook, disjoint wave-2 scopes. B has a concrete conflict: agents E and F each write "half of views.test.jsx" — two parallel agents editing one file — plus four sequential waves and the SSE seam (7). C's four wave-1 agents own disjoint files including per-agent CSS scopes (overview.css/detail.css/charts.css), but agent C's scope is heavy (shell + overview + 3 hooks + 4 components) and its Overview imports chart files agent B is writing simultaneously, and mixed .js server importing shared/contract.ts (dayKey) is an unaddressed Node/TS seam (8). Depth: B leads slightly (cross-filter, palette, sparklines, 8) with C close behind (keyboard-driven Gazetteer, search/sort, hover annotations, dual themes that are "a second look, not a second design", 7). Coherence: A and C both 9 — C's single survey-folio identity enforced by a frozen Plate component and tokens-only audit is the strongest anti-drift design of the three. On totals A and B tie at 38 and C clears both at 43; per the tiebreak instruction the buildable A would beat B, but neither reaches C.

steals.what: Heatmap day-click cross-filter: clicking a day cell filters the timeline and surfaces that day's commits ('what was I doing on March 12th') — graft onto C's Fig. 2/Fig. 3 plates as a margin-annotation interaction.

Injectable transport in the SSE hook with a polling fallback — EventSource does not exist in jsdom, so C's useAtlas should take a transport parameter so hooks.test.tsx mounts cleanly and the UI degrades gracefully if SSE drops.

A canonical shared fixture Snapshot module as the single test-data source for all client tests (C only has chart-level fixtures); plus a contract-lock test asserting enum values and comparator ordering never drift.

An explicit fixture test pinning the rev-list --left-right --count parse order — an inverted parse makes behind-only repos show as 'unpushed', silently breaking the attention queue's most trusted signal.
Pin TZ in the vitest config for the author-date day-bucketing tests — otherwise a UTC-string-slicing implementation passes on the build machine while mislabeling days for the user.
Cmd+K fuzzy repo-jump palette layered on top of C's j/k navigation — two keystrokes to any repo's drill-down beats scrolling the Gazetteer once the repo count is in the dozens.
